name: Galvanized Eye Lag Screw
title: Galvanized Eye Lag Screw for Tree Cabling
meta: Galvanized eye lag screw for light tree cabling and guying. How lag eyes anchor a cable, when to use a through-bolt instead, and how to install them cleanly.
tagline: A galvanized lag eye for anchoring light cable systems in small to medium limbs.
summary: This galvanized eye lag screw threads straight into sound wood and gives you a closed eye to terminate a cable on. It is the simple anchor for light cabling jobs in smaller leads where a through-bolt would be overkill. The galvanized finish holds up to weather while the tree closes wood around the shank.
highlights: Closed eye for terminating cable with a thimble or dead-end
Lag (wood screw) thread bites into sound wood
Galvanized steel resists rust in the canopy
Installs from one side with a pilot hole and a bar through the eye
Suited to light cabling in smaller-diameter leads
specs: Light-duty cable anchors in small to medium leads
Install per ANSI A300 Part 3 and the hardware maker's instructions

body.h: What an eye lag screw does in a cable system
p: A cable system is only as good as its anchors. The galvanized eye lag screw is the lightest anchor in the cabling kit: you drill a pilot hole, thread the lag into sound wood until the eye sits just proud of the bark, and terminate your cable on the eye with a thimble or a preformed dead-end.

Because it goes in from one side, a lag eye is quick to set from a climbing position or out of a bucket. That makes it a good fit for light cabling in younger trees and smaller codominant leads, where you want support without drilling all the way through the stem.
Browse the rest of the anchors, cable and dead-ends in our cabling hardware section.

Lag eyes are also handy beyond cabling. Crews use them to anchor guying on transplanted trees, to hang a light support for a leaning ornamental, or as a fixed point for a brace on a fence line tree. In each case the logic is the same: sound wood, a straight pilot hole, and a load that pulls in line with the shank.

Lags rely on thread engagement in the wood, so they are rated lower than a through-bolt with a washer and nut on the far side. On bigger leads, heavier loads, or wood with any question about soundness, step up to a through-bolt or a J-lag sized for the job.

Read the load ratings published by the hardware maker and match the anchor to the cable you are installing. The current reference for cabling and bracing in the US is ANSI A300 Part 3. If you are new to cabling, learn it from someone who installs systems regularly before you put a lag in a client's tree.

Think about the whole system, not just the anchor. Cable, termination and anchor should all be sized to work together, and the weakest piece sets the real capacity. A heavy cable on a light lag gives you a false sense of security.

Drill a pilot hole sized to the lag's root diameter, in line with the direction the cable will pull. A lag set at an angle to the cable gets side-loaded at the eye. Thread it in with a bar through the eye and stop when the eye is just clear of the bark so the tree can grow without engulfing the termination too soon.

Inspect the tree before you drill. Do not set anchors in decay, cracks or included bark. Plan to re-inspect the system on a regular schedule, because trees grow, cables loosen, and hardware that was right five years ago may need adjustment.

Keep a small kit together for cabling days: a selection of lag eyes, a long auger bit sized for the pilot, a bar or large screwdriver to turn the eye, thimbles, dead-ends and a tape to measure the leads. Having it all in one bag means fewer trips down the rope.

Write down what you installed, where, and when. A simple record on the work order lets the next inspection check that the anchor, cable and tension are still doing their job, and gives the client a reason to have the system looked at on schedule.

faq.q: What size eye lag screw should I use for tree cabling?
faq.a: Size the lag to the cable and the lead. Lags are for light systems in smaller leads. Check the maker's ratings and ANSI A300 Part 3, and move to a through-bolt when the load or limb size calls for it.

faq.q: Do I need a pilot hole for a lag eye?
faq.a: Yes. Drill a pilot hole close to the root diameter of the thread so the lag pulls in straight without splitting the wood or stripping out.

faq.q: How far should the eye stick out from the bark?
faq.a: Leave the eye just clear of the bark. Too far out adds leverage on the shank; flush means the tree swallows the termination quickly.

faq.q: Can I use a hardware-store eye screw instead?
faq.a: Use hardware sold for tree support with published ratings. Light-duty eye screws with bent or open eyes are not made for the loads a cable system sees.

name: J-Lag Screws
title: J-Lag Screws for Tree Cabling: Sizes and Install Tips
meta: J-lag screws give a cable system a hook-style anchor set into the lead. How they compare with eye lags, lag studs and through-bolts, and how to set them.
tagline: Hook-style lag anchors for cabling leads with a cable that wraps the J.
summary: J-lag screws are threaded tree cabling anchors with an open J-shaped hook in place of a closed eye. You drill a pilot hole, thread the J-lag into sound wood, and seat the cable termination over the hook. Arborists like them because the cable can be hooked on after the anchor is set.
highlights: Open J hook lets you seat the termination after the anchor is in
Lag thread installs from one side of the lead
Galvanized finish for long service outdoors
Pairs with thimbles and preformed dead-ends
Faster to set than a through-bolt on light systems
specs: Install per ANSI A300 Part 3 and maker's instructions

body.h: How J-lags fit into a cabling job
p: On a typical cabling job you set one anchor in each lead, then run cable between them about two-thirds of the way from the weak union to the tops of the leads. A J-lag gives you a hook to drop the thimbled cable end onto, which makes tensioning and final termination easier when you are working alone in the canopy.
Because it installs from one side, a J-lag saves you drilling through the whole lead. That is a real advantage on light systems in younger trees, where you want to keep wounding to a minimum.

J-lags also suit retrofit work. When an existing system needs a second cable or a replacement run, a hook anchor lets you set hardware, then bring the new cable to it and hang the termination without threading anything through a closed eye.
Keep the hardware matched: J-lag, thimble, dead-end and cable from systems that are meant to work together, with published ratings for each part.

body.h: J-lag, eye lag or lag stud
p: A closed eye lag screw holds the termination captive. A J-lag lets you hook on after the fact, but the termination must stay seated against the hook. A lag stud, also called a lag-threaded rod, has lag thread on one end and machine thread on the other so you can add an amon-eye nut. All three rely on thread grip in the wood.

None of them match a through-bolt with a nut and washer on the far side for holding power. Choose the anchor by the published rating, the size of the lead and the load you expect, and follow ANSI A300 Part 3.

Drill the pilot hole in line with the cable so the hook pulls straight. Thread the J-lag in until the hook sits just clear of the bark, with the open side facing away from the cable's pull so the termination cannot slip off.

Inspect the wood before drilling and stay out of decay, cracks and included bark. Re-inspect cable systems on a schedule; growth and storms change what the system is doing. If you are learning cabling, get supervised experience first.
Clean up after yourself: brush shavings out of the hole before threading, and keep the work order notes clear on which lead got which anchor.

body.h: Inspection over the life of the system
p: Every cable system needs follow-up. Leads grow, cables slacken or tighten, and storms can shift a termination off a hook if it was not seated properly. Put the tree on an inspection schedule and note the hardware type and install date on the work order.

On a re-inspection, look for the hook opening, any wear where the thimble rides, wood swelling over the J, and cracks or decay near the anchor. If the tree has outgrown a light system, replace it with heavier hardware rather than adding more of the same.

faq.q: Which way should the hook of a J-lag face?
faq.a: Orient it so the cable pulls the termination into the bottom of the J, with the opening away from the line of pull.

faq.q: Are J-lags as strong as through-bolts?
faq.a: No. Lag anchors depend on thread grip in wood. Use through-bolts for heavier loads or larger leads.

faq.q: What is a lag stud?
faq.a: A rod with lag thread on one end and machine thread on the other. It takes an amon-eye nut, giving you an adjustable eye on a lag anchor.

faq.q: Do J-lags need a pilot hole?
faq.a: Yes. Drill a pilot close to the thread's root diameter so the lag goes in straight and grips well.

name: Lac Balsam Tree Wound Treatment
title: Lac Balsam Tree Wound Treatment: When It Makes Sense
meta: Lac Balsam tree wound dressing is a water-based, brush-on coating for bark wounds. Where it is useful, where it is not, and what current pruning standards say.
tagline: A brush-on, water-based tree wound dressing for bark damage and grafts.
summary: Lac Balsam is a water-based tree wound dressing that you brush onto damaged bark, where it dries to a flexible film. Arborists and orchard growers use it on bark tears, mower damage and graft unions rather than on routine pruning cuts.
highlights: Water-based, cleans up with water
Brushes on and dries to a flexible coating
Used on bark tears, equipment damage and grafts
Not needed on routine, well-made pruning cuts

p: Most current guidance, including ANSI A300, says wound dressings are not needed on ordinary pruning cuts. A good cut at the branch collar closes on its own. Lac Balsam earns its place on the jobs where you want to protect exposed cambium: a strip of bark torn off by a mower or a lowering mishap, a fresh graft, or a wound on a young tree you are trying to keep moist.
It is a niche product. If a client asks for wound paint on every cut, explain the standard and save the dressing for the cases above.

Some growers also like it on grafts, where it helps keep the union from drying out while the scion takes. On young street trees damaged during planting or by string trimmers, a coat can protect the wound while you sort out the cause, usually by mulching a ring so the trimmer stays away.

Trim loose, ragged bark back to clean, attached tissue first. Brush a thin layer over the exposed wood and the wound edges, then let it dry. Check the product label for temperature limits and reapplication. Wash brushes in water before it sets.

A tub goes a long way since you only coat damaged areas. Keep the lid sealed between uses so it does not skin over, and store it where it will not freeze. If a wound keeps getting reopened, fix the cause; no dressing replaces good care.

faq.q: Is Lac Balsam the same as Lak Balsam?
faq.a: Yes. Lak Balsam is a common misspelling of Lac Balsam, the same water-based wound dressing.

faq.q: Should I put Lac Balsam on every pruning cut?
faq.a: No. Standard practice is to leave proper pruning cuts undressed. Use it on bark damage, grafts and similar wounds.

name: Tree Support Web for Staking Trees, 250 ft
title: Tree Support Web for Staking Trees, 250 ft Roll
h1: Tree Support Web for Staking Trees
meta: Soft tree support web for staking newly planted trees. Wide webbing holds a tree to its stakes without girdling bark. Tips for stake support and removal timing.
tagline: Soft, wide staking web on a roll for supporting newly planted trees.
summary: This tree support web is a soft strap on a long roll for tying newly planted trees to their stakes. Wide webbing spreads the load on the bark, so the tree gets support without the cutting and girdling you get from wire or narrow twine.
highlights: Wide, soft webbing that does not cut into bark
Long roll for crews planting many trees
Cut to length for each tree and stake
Allows some trunk movement, which builds taper
Easy to remove when the stakes come out
specs: Tie trees to stakes after planting
Loose figure-eight or loop around trunk and stake

body.h: Why use a web instead of wire
p: A newly planted tree with a small root ball can rock in the wind before the roots grab the surrounding soil. Staking gives it a little help. The tie is where most staking goes wrong: wire, even inside a hose section, and thin twine can cut into the bark and girdle the trunk if they are forgotten.

A wide tree support web spreads the pressure over a larger patch of bark. It holds the trunk steady without clamping it. On a planting crew, a 250 ft roll goes a long way, since each tie only needs a short length.
The web is also kinder to the crew. It is easy to cut, quick to tie, and soft enough that nobody is fighting stiff wire with pliers on a planting day.

body.h: Setting up stake support for trees
p: Drive two or three stakes outside the root ball, not through it. Attach the web to each stake and loop it around the trunk loosely, low enough that the top of the tree can still sway. Some movement is good; it is what tells the trunk to add taper and strength.

Tie a loose figure-eight between trunk and stake so the web does not rub the bark. Keep the attachment at the stake tight and the loop at the trunk relaxed. For larger trees on windy sites, guying with cable and earth anchors may be a better choice; see our planting supplies.
On sites with mowers and trimmers, keep stakes and web where they can be seen. Bright stakes or a mulch ring keep equipment off the trunk while the tree establishes.

Look at staked trees a few times through the season. Loosen anything that has tightened, and check for rubbing. Most trees can lose their stakes after one growing season once the roots have established. Leaving support on for years does the tree no favors.
Cut the web off cleanly rather than leaving it wrapped on the trunk. Forgotten ties are one of the most common reasons young street trees fail.
If bark under the tie has been rubbed raw, move the loop to fresh bark and loosen it. Small marks heal; deep rubbing does not.

body.h: Staking as part of good planting
p: Staking is a small part of getting a tree established. Planting at the right depth, with the root flare visible, mulched and watered through the first season, does far more for a tree than any tie. Treat the stake and web as a short-term aid, not a fix for a poorly planted tree.

For trees where you are unsure, try planting without stakes and keep an eye on them after the first few storms. If one starts to lean or rock, add support then. Many trees establish faster when left to move freely from the start.

faq.q: How long should a tree stay staked?
faq.a: Usually one growing season. Check root establishment and remove the stakes and web as soon as the tree stands on its own.

faq.q: How tight should a tree support web be?
faq.a: Snug at the stake and loose at the trunk, so the tree can sway a little without rubbing.

faq.q: Does every new tree need staking?
faq.a: No. Many container and balled trees stand fine without it. Stake only when the tree is top-heavy, the site is windy, or people are likely to push on it.

name: Wire Rope Clamps
title: Wire Rope Clamps: Sizes, Spacing and Correct Install
meta: Galvanized wire rope clamps for tree guying and cable work. How to size a wire rope clip, which side the saddle goes on, and why torque and count matter.
tagline: Galvanized U-bolt wire rope clips for guying trees and making eyes in cable.
summary: Wire rope clamps, also called wire rope clips or cable clamps, let you form an eye or join wire cable without swaging tools. On tree jobs they show up when guying newly planted trees to earth anchors or making temporary cable terminations. They are cheap and simple, but only work when installed the right way around and torqued.
highlights: U-bolt and saddle design, the classic wire rope clip
Galvanized finish for outdoor service
Sized to match the cable diameter
No swaging or special tools, just a wrench
Used with thimbles to protect the cable eye
specs: Match clip size to cable diameter
Per maker's table for each size

body.h: Where wire rope clamps fit on tree jobs
p: In the planting world, wire cable clamps are the quick way to terminate guy cable on larger transplanted trees: cable from a collar on the trunk, down to an earth anchor, with a thimbled eye clamped at each end. They also come in handy for temporary cable work around the yard and shop.
For permanent tree cabling inside the canopy, preformed dead-ends are the usual termination. Pair clamps with duckbill earth anchors when you are guying from the ground.
Around the shop, clamps also hold a cable on a winch line or make a quick eye on a sling for dragging logs. Keep a few sizes in the truck with matching thimbles.

The U-bolt goes on the dead end, the short tail. The saddle sits on the live end, the side that carries the load. Install a clip backward and the U-bolt crushes the loaded cable and cuts its strength a lot. Every clip on the run goes the same way.
Use a thimble in the eye so the cable does not kink around a tight bend. Put the first clip one saddle-width from the dead end, the next tight against the thimble, and any others evenly between.

Seat the cable fully into the thimble groove before tightening the first clip, and keep the thimble from rotating or falling out as you go. A loose thimble lets the eye collapse under load. Tighten the nuts evenly, alternating sides, so the saddle pulls down square on the cable rather than cocking to one side.
Use the right size. An oversized clip will not grip a small cable, and an undersized one will not close over the larger cable at all.

Each size has a minimum number of clips, a turnback length and a torque value published by the maker. Small cables usually need at least two clips and larger ones more. Follow the table that ships with the clamps rather than guessing.

Torque the nuts, put the cable under load, then retorque. Cable stretches and settles, and loose clips let the cable slip. Check guyed trees through the season and remove guying once the tree has rooted in.

Keep spare clamps dry and the threads clean. A rusty, galled thread will not reach the right torque, and that means a termination that can slip. Replace any clamp with a bent U-bolt or cracked saddle.
When you take a guy system down, inspect the cable where the clips sat. Crushed or kinked cable should not go back into service; cut it off and start fresh.

A clipped termination does not reach the full strength of the cable. That is fine for guying a tree. Do not use clipped terminations in life-support systems or as a substitute for rated rigging hardware.

faq.q: What is the difference between a wire rope clamp and a wire rope clip?
faq.a: Nothing. Wire rope clamp, wire rope clip and cable clamp all describe the same U-bolt and saddle fitting.

faq.q: Which side does the saddle go on?
faq.a: The saddle goes on the live, load-bearing side of the cable. The U-bolt goes on the dead-end tail.

faq.q: How many clamps do I need?
faq.a: It depends on cable size. Use the maker's table; small cables generally take at least two clips, larger cables more.

faq.q: Do I need to retighten wire rope clamps?
faq.a: Yes. Retorque after the first load and check them periodically.

name: Duckbill Earth Anchors, Small
title: Small Duckbill Anchors for Guying Newly Planted Trees
h1: Small Duckbill Anchors for Tree Guying
meta: Small duckbill anchors for guying newly planted trees. How duckbill earth anchors drive and set, how many to use per tree, and what to check during the season.
tagline: Drive-in earth anchors for guying smaller newly planted trees.
summary: Small duckbill anchors are drive-in earth anchors that let you guy a newly planted tree without wooden stakes. You drive the anchor into the ground with a drive rod, pull back on the cable, and the anchor turns sideways in the soil and locks. They are quick to set and out of the way once installed.
highlights: Drive-in installation with a steel drive rod
Anchor rotates and locks when you pull the cable
Low profile, nothing for mowers to catch
Small size for smaller caliper trees
Use three anchors around the tree for even support
specs: Drive rod, then load-lock by pulling up
Three anchors spaced around the tree
Depends on soil type; see maker's chart

p: A duckbill earth anchor looks like a small metal bill with a cable attached. You set it on the end of a drive rod and hammer it into the ground at an angle away from the tree. Pull the rod out, then pull up hard on the cable. The anchor pivots crosswise in the soil, like a toggle bolt in drywall, and resists further pulling.
That load-lock step matters. An anchor that has not turned holds very little. Pull until you feel it set before attaching the guy to the tree.

The design is simple and that is the appeal. There are no stakes sticking up for kids or mowers to hit, and the only thing left above ground is the guy cable running to the trunk. On a commercial planting with many trees, a crew can set a set of duckbill earth anchors in minutes per tree.

For most trees, three duckbill anchors spaced evenly around the root ball give support from every direction. Keep the anchors outside the root ball, and run each guy to a soft collar or strap on the trunk, never bare wire on bark.
Leave a little slack so the tree can move. Terminate the cable with a thimble and wire rope clamps or the hardware supplied in a duckbill anchor kit.

Angle the guys so they meet the trunk at roughly one-third to two-thirds of its height, with the anchor far enough out to give a reasonable angle. Flag the guys with tape or covers so people do not walk into them.

Holding power depends on soil. Dense clay holds well; loose sand and wet soil hold less. Small anchors are for small trees. For larger caliper trees, step up to a bigger anchor size and check the maker's chart.
Call before you dig. Driving anchors into buried utility lines is a real hazard, so get locates done first.

A duckbill anchor kit typically includes the anchors with cable attached and the hardware to terminate them. Check what your kit includes and whether you need a drive rod, which is reusable and worth keeping in the truck.
Plan to remove guys after a season or so, once the roots have established. Cut the cable at ground level and leave the anchor in place, or dig it out if the site needs it clear.

If the tree still moves too much at removal time, check the planting depth and root ball before you add the guys back. Guying cannot fix a tree planted too deep or a root ball that has fallen apart. Note anchor locations on the work order so the next crew knows where the cable runs are, especially near lawns that get aerated.

faq.q: How deep do small duckbill anchors go?
faq.a: Drive them to the depth the maker specifies for the size, then load-lock. Deeper generally holds better in firm soil.

faq.q: How many duckbill anchors per tree?
faq.a: Three, spaced evenly around the tree, is the common setup.

faq.q: Can I reuse duckbill anchors?
faq.a: They are generally treated as single-use once set. Cut the cable and leave the anchor buried when removing guys.

name: Distel Replacement Pads with Rings and Straps
title: Distel Replacement Pads with Rings and Straps
h1: Distel Replacement Pads with Rings and Straps
meta: Distel replacement pads with rings and straps refresh a worn set of Distel climbers. When to replace pads and straps, and what to inspect before the next climb.
tagline: Fresh pads, rings and straps to put worn Distel climbers back in service.
summary: Distel replacement pads with rings and straps let you rebuild the upper end of your Distel climbers when the old pads are cracked, compressed or the straps are worn. New pads restore comfort on long removals and keep the spur seated on your leg.
highlights: Made to fit Distel tree climbers
Pads, rings and straps in one set
Restores comfort and fit on worn spurs
Cheaper than replacing the whole climber

body.h: When to replace pads and straps
p: Pads take a beating on removals. Once the foam is flattened, the leather is cracking, or the straps are stretched, frayed or cut, it is time to rebuild. Worn straps let the spur roll on your leg, and that is how gaffs cut out of the bark.
Swapping in Distel pads with new rings and straps is a straightforward job at the truck. Confirm the set matches your climber model before you order.

Replacing pads is also a chance to improve fit. If you have changed boots or the old straps never sat right, take the time to set the new ones up properly, with buckles where they do not dig in and strap tails secured so they do not catch.
Order the set once you know your model and size so the swap is a one-trip job.

While the pads are off, look over the shank and the gaff. Check for bends, cracks and loose hardware, and sharpen or replace dull gaffs following Distel's guidance. Browse replacement gaffs and parts for the rest. Spurs are for removals; climb with a properly rated lanyard and climbing system per ANSI Z133.
Remember that gaffs only belong in trees that are coming down. Spurs wound live trees, so climb on rope for pruning work.

faq.q: Will these pads fit other brands of climbers?
faq.a: They are made for Distel climbers. Fit on other brands is not assured.

faq.q: How do I know my straps need replacing?
faq.a: Replace straps that are cut, frayed, stretched, stiff or have damaged buckles or stitching.

name: Speed Line Kit with Carabiners
title: Arborist Speed Line Kit with Carabiners
h1: Arborist Speed Line Kit with Carabiners
meta: Arborist speed line kit with carabiners for zipping brush and wood out of the tree. How a speedline is rigged, tensioned and anchored, plus safe working limits.
tagline: A speedline setup for zipping brush and wood over obstacles to the drop zone.
summary: This speed line kit gives you the line and connectors to run brush and light wood down a tensioned rope from the canopy to a drop zone away from the tree. It is the setup arborists reach for when the landing area is full of roofs, fences and gardens.
highlights: Moves brush away from targets below the tree
Locking carabiners for clipping loads to the line
Faster cleanup with brush landing in one pile
Works with a pulley or carabiners riding the line
Pairs with a lowering device for tensioning and control
specs: High anchor in tree, low anchor at drop zone
Mechanical advantage or lowering device at the low anchor

p: A speedline is a rope run at an angle from a high anchor in the tree to a low anchor on the ground away from the tree. The climber clips cut brush to the line with a carabiner or pulley and it slides down to the landing zone. Ground crew unclip it and drag it to the chipper.
It turns a tight backyard removal into a steady flow of brush to one spot. Instead of lowering every limb to a crowded drop zone under the tree, you send it over the shed and onto the driveway.

Anchor the high end in a sound part of the tree above the work. Anchor the low end to a solid object: another tree, a stump, or the truck if your company allows it. Tension the line with a mechanical advantage system or by taking wraps on a lowering device. Too tight and you overload anchors; too slack and loads drag through the targets.
Use locking carabiners or a pulley to ride the line. A few loads in, check the anchors and retension. For a ready-to-go system from a known maker, compare this with the Weaver speed line kit.

Pick the angle with care. Too steep and loads arrive fast and hit hard; too shallow and they stall halfway. A controlled line, where a ground worker can hold a friction wrap on the low end, gives you the option to slow or stop a load.

Clip the carabiner to the line first, then to the brush, usually through a sling or around the butt of the branch. Keep loads small enough for the line and the anchors. Heavy wood on a speedline puts high forces on the top anchor.
Have a tag line or control line on anything that could swing. Ground crew stays clear of the line's path and the landing zone until the load stops.

Small, frequent loads are the rule. Several light bundles put far less stress on the anchors than one large limb, and they are easier for the ground crew to handle at the landing zone. Strip side branches from bulky brush so it rides cleanly instead of dragging through shrubs on the way down.
Keep extra carabiners on the line so the climber can send the next load while the ground crew is still unhooking the last one. A rope bag or bucket at the bottom collects returned connectors.

A speedline is rigging, not life support. Never clip yourself to it. Inspect rope, slings and carabiners before use and retire damaged gear. Work to ANSI Z133 and get trained on speedline setup before you run one over targets.
Brief the ground crew before the first load. Agree on calls for sending, clear and stop, and keep everyone out from under the line while brush is moving.

faq.q: What knot should I use to attach a line to a carabiner?
faq.a: For rigging, a figure-eight on a bight or a bowline clipped into a locking carabiner is common. Use a knot you have been trained to tie and inspect, and dress it before loading.

faq.q: How tight should a speedline be?
faq.a: Tight enough that loads clear the targets, no tighter. Over-tensioning multiplies the forces on both anchors.

faq.q: Can I use a pulley instead of a carabiner on the line?
faq.a: Yes. A pulley runs faster and with less wear on the line. Carabiners slow loads down, which can help on steep lines.

name: Rock Exotica Downrigger
title: Rock Exotica Downrigger Rigging Pulley
meta: The Rock Exotica Downrigger is a rigging pulley for redirecting lowering lines. What a downrigger is used for on tree removals and how to set and inspect it.
tagline: A rigging pulley for redirecting and managing lowering lines on removals.
summary: The Rock Exotica Downrigger is a rigging pulley built for the lowering side of tree work, where you need to redirect a line cleanly and keep friction where you want it. Rock Exotica builds its hardware for rope access and rescue, and this pulley brings that build quality to arborist rigging.
highlights: Rigging pulley from Rock Exotica
Redirects lowering lines with low rope wear
Clips into a sling or anchor with a carabiner
Machined hardware with clear markings
specs: Marked on the device; follow maker's instructions

body.h: What is a downrigger used for?
p: In tree work, a downrigger setup is about controlling where the lowering line runs. Hung from a sling in the tree, a pulley like this redirects the line so the load swings away from targets, or so the ground worker gets a better angle to the lowering device at the base.
It sees real dynamic forces when a piece is caught, so treat it as rigging hardware and size the rest of the system to match.

A redirect also keeps the lowering line off bark and out of tight crotches where it would wear. On big removals, a well-placed pulley can turn an awkward drop straight into the yard into a clean, controlled descent onto the lawn. Plan the angle before the first cut and check it once the first piece is down.

Hang the pulley from a sling choked or girth-hitched to a sound, well-sized part of the tree, and connect with a locking carabiner of suitable strength. Keep the line running in the sheave without rubbing the side plates.

Before each job, check that the sheave spins freely, the side plates close and lock, and there are no cracks, deep scores or rope burns. Retire hardware that has been shock loaded beyond its rating or dropped from height onto a hard surface. Rigging is not life support; keep it separate from your climbing system and work to ANSI Z133.

faq.q: What is a downrigger used for in tree rigging?
faq.a: It redirects the lowering line so loads come down where you want them and the ground worker has a clean angle to the friction device.

faq.q: Can I climb on a rigging pulley?
faq.a: Do not mix rigging and life-support gear. Use climbing hardware rated and intended for life support, per the maker's instructions.

name: CMI 5/8" Steel Arborist Block
title: CMI 5/8" Steel Arborist Block for Rigging
meta: CMI 5/8 in steel arborist block for rigging lines on removals. Where a steel-sheave arborist block fits, how to hang it, and what to inspect before every job.
tagline: A steel-sheave rigging block for 5/8 in lowering lines on removal work.
summary: The CMI 5/8 in steel arborist block is a rigging block for lowering wood on 5/8 in rope. A steel sheave stands up to the heat and wear of repeated heavy lowering, and CMI hardware has a long record in rope rescue and tree work.
highlights: Sized for rigging lines up to 5/8 in
Steel sheave for durability under heavy use
Hangs from a sling high in the tree
Built by CMI, a long-time rescue hardware maker

p: An arborist block is the top of a natural crotch alternative: hung from a sling above the work, it gives the rigging line a smooth, low-friction path. That cuts rope wear and puts the friction where it belongs, at the lowering device on the trunk, so the ground worker can let pieces run and stop them smoothly.
A 5/8 in block suits crews running 5/8 in rigging line for medium to heavy wood.

Steel adds weight compared with aluminum, but for a block that stays rigged in one place through a removal, durability is worth more than a few ounces. Pair it with a sling and lowering device rated to match.
It also suits crews who rig hard every day and want a block that outlasts the rope running through it.

Hang it on a properly rated sling, girth hitched or choked high enough to clear the piece, with the line running straight through the sheave. Keep the block above the cut so forces stay in line with the stem.

Before every job check that the sheave turns freely, side plates are straight and close properly, and there are no cracks or deformation. Retire a block that has been overloaded. Rigging gear must be kept separate from climbing gear, and crews should be trained to ANSI Z133.

faq.q: What size rope fits this arborist block?
faq.a: It is sized for rigging lines up to 5/8 in diameter. Smaller lines will run but larger ones will not.

faq.q: Why use a steel sheave?
faq.a: Steel resists wear and heat better than aluminum under repeated heavy lowering.

name: ISC Small Rigging Pulley for up to 5/8" Rope
title: ISC Small Rigging Pulley for up to 5/8" Rope
h1: ISC Small Rigging Pulley for up to 5/8" Rope
meta: ISC small rigging pulley for rope up to 5/8 in. A compact pulley for light rigging, redirects and pull lines, with tips on where it fits and what to inspect.
tagline: A compact ISC pulley for light rigging and redirects on lines up to 5/8 in.
summary: The ISC small rigging pulley takes rope up to 5/8 in and packs a lot of capability into a small, light pulley. It is the one to carry for light rigging, redirects on pull lines and mechanical advantage setups where a full-size block is more than you need.
highlights: Fits rope up to 5/8 in
Compact and light to carry on the saddle
Good for redirects and light rigging
ISC build quality from a rope-access hardware maker

body.h: Where a small rigging pulley earns its place
p: Not every piece needs a big block. A small rigging pulley handles light limbs, redirects a pull line around an obstacle, or acts as the moving pulley in a mechanical advantage system for tensioning a speedline or pulling over a small tree. Because it is light, it rides on the saddle without being in the way.
Keep heavier wood on a full-size block rated for the forces involved.

Small pulleys also help on the ground. Anchor one to a stump to turn a pull line so the crew can pull from a safe spot outside the fall zone, or use it to change the angle on a winch line. Having one in the rigging bag saves improvising with a carabiner, which adds friction and wears the rope.

Clip it to a sling or anchor with a locking carabiner and keep the rope running cleanly in the sheave. Check the sheave and side plates before each use, and retire the pulley after a severe shock load or visible damage.
Rigging gear is not life support. Keep it separate from climbing gear, follow ISC's instructions, and work to ANSI Z133.
Wash out grit after muddy jobs; dirt in the bearing slows the sheave and wears the rope.

faq.q: Can I use smaller cord in this pulley?
faq.a: Smaller rope will run, but the sheave is designed for larger rigging lines. Very thin cord can jam between sheave and side plate, so use a pulley sized for it.

faq.q: Is this pulley for heavy rigging?
faq.a: It is meant for light rigging and redirects. Use a full-size block for heavy wood.

name: Petzl PAW Small Rigging Plate
title: Petzl PAW Small Rigging Plate for Anchors
meta: The Petzl PAW S rigging plate turns one anchor into several clean connection points. How arborists use a small rigging plate for SRT anchors and redirects.
tagline: A small aluminum rigging plate for organizing carabiners at an anchor.
summary: The Petzl PAW S is a small rigging plate that gives one anchor several neat connection points. Clip it to a sling or base anchor and you can hang a rope, a redirect and a backup without stacking carabiners on top of each other.
highlights: Multiple holes for separate carabiners
Keeps connectors from cross-loading each other
Small, light aluminum plate
Useful for base-tied SRT anchors and rescue setups

p: Stacking carabiners on a single connector leads to cross-loading and a mess you cannot sort out quickly. A rigging plate spreads connections across separate holes. For an arborist, that might mean a base-anchored SRT line, a rescue line and a redirect all off one sling at the base of the tree, each on its own carabiner.
The Petzl PAW is a common choice among rope-access workers, and the small size is the right fit for most tree setups.

It also helps on removals with a rescue plan in place: the rescue line hangs ready on its own hole instead of buried under the working connections. Everyone on the crew can see at a glance what is clipped where, which matters when things need to happen fast.

Clip the plate to the anchor through its top hole and load each lower hole with a single carabiner. Inspect for cracks, sharp edges and wear grooves before use. Life-support gear must be used per the maker's instructions and inspected, and climbers should be trained before setting up base anchors.

Pick carabiners that sit well in the plate holes and rotate freely. A connector jammed against the edge of a hole can be side-loaded. Keep the plate in your climbing kit rather than the rigging bag so it does not see the abuse rigging hardware takes.

faq.q: What is the Petzl PAW used for?
faq.a: It organizes several carabiners at one anchor so each connection hangs separately and loads cleanly.

faq.q: Can a rigging plate be part of a climbing system?
faq.a: Yes, if used per Petzl's instructions and within its rating. Inspect it before each use.

name: Double Swing Pulley
title: Double Swing Pulley for a Double Pulley System
h1: Double Swing Pulley for a Double Pulley System
meta: Double swing pulley for a compact double pulley system: haul lines, pull lines and tensioning. How to rig a 2 pulley system and what to check before use.
tagline: A two-sheave swing-side pulley for building compact mechanical advantage systems.
summary: A double pulley puts two sheaves side by side in one frame, and this double swing pulley has side plates that open so you can load rope mid-line. It is the building block for a compact double pulley system: pulling over a tree, tensioning a speedline or hauling a heavy piece out of a ditch.
highlights: Two sheaves in one frame for compact haul systems
Swing-open side plates let you load rope mid-line
Pairs with a second pulley for higher ratios
Useful for pull lines, speedlines and log handling
Clips to an anchor with a single locking carabiner
specs: Single attachment point for a carabiner

body.h: What a double pulley system does
p: Mechanical advantage lets one or two people put serious force on a rope. With two double pulleys, one anchored and one on the load, you can build a 4:1 system in a compact package. Add a progress capture or a friction hitch and you can hold what you gain. A single double pulley paired with a single pulley gives you a 3:1.
On tree jobs that means pulling a back-leaning tree over the notch, tensioning a speedline, or skidding a heavy log onto the trailer without a winch.

The compact frame matters in the field. Two single pulleys hanging side by side twist around each other and tangle; a double pulley keeps both rope parts in one plane and runs cleaner. Fewer separate pieces also means fewer carabiners to manage, which speeds setup and teardown on a busy day.

With fixed side plates you have to thread the rope through from the end. That is slow when the rope is already rigged with a running end tied off a hundred feet away. Swing plates let you open the pulley, drop the rope in, close it and clip it, all at the middle of the line.
Check that the plates close fully and the carabiner passes through both before loading. A pulley that is not closed can let the rope ride out under load.
Swing plates also make teardown fast. Once the pull is done, open the plates, lift the rope out and pack the pulley without pulling a hundred feet of line back through.

The simplest 2 pulley system is a single pulley at the anchor and one at the load: rope tied off at one pulley, through the other and back, gives you 2:1 or 3:1 depending on where the end is tied. A double pulley at each end doubles the number of rope parts and the ratio.

Friction in each sheave eats into the theoretical advantage, so real-world output is less than the math says. Good bearings and correct rope diameter help. Keep ropes from twisting around each other between the pulleys, which adds friction fast.
More of the haul hardware is in our mechanical advantage section.

Mechanical advantage can easily overload anchors, slings and the tree itself. Know the forces you are making, and use hardware rated for them. When pulling trees over, keep everyone clear of the fall zone and the line's path if something breaks. Rigging gear is not life support; keep it separate from climbing gear and train crews to ANSI Z133.
Inspect the pulley before each job: sheaves spin freely, no cracks or bends, side plates tight on the axle.
Store it clean and dry, and keep it in the rigging bag rather than loose in the truck bed.

faq.q: What ratio can I get with a double pulley?
faq.a: Two double pulleys rigged together give 4:1 theoretical advantage, or 5:1 if the rope end is tied to the moving pulley. Friction reduces the real output.

faq.q: What is the difference between a double pulley and a tandem pulley?
faq.a: A double pulley has two sheaves side by side for mechanical advantage. A tandem pulley has two sheaves in line to ride a tensioned rope.

faq.q: Do I need progress capture?
faq.a: For hauling and tensioning it is strongly recommended. A friction hitch or progress-capture pulley holds the load when you reset.

name: Petzl Tandem Pulley
title: Petzl Tandem Pulley for Speedlines and Tyroleans
meta: The Petzl Tandem pulley runs two sheaves in line to ride a tensioned rope. How arborists use a tandem pulley on speedlines and how it compares to other pulleys.
tagline: A two-sheave in-line pulley for riding tensioned lines and speedlines.
summary: The Petzl Tandem pulley has two sheaves in line so it rides a tensioned rope smoothly, which is why it shows up on speedlines and tyrolean traverses. Among Petzl pulleys, it is the one built for moving along a line rather than redirecting one.
highlights: Two in-line sheaves for riding a tensioned rope
Smooth travel on speedlines
Side plates open to install mid-line
Light, compact Petzl build

body.h: Using a tandem pulley on a speedline
p: On a speedline, brush hung from a single pulley tends to tip and drag. A tandem pulley spreads the load along two sheaves, so it tracks straight and runs fast. Clip the brush to the pulley with a sling and locking carabiner and let it go.
Line angle and tension decide how fast loads arrive. Have a plan for stopping them at the bottom.

The side plates open so you can install it on the line without untying, which saves time when each load needs its own pulley. Many crews keep several on the line so the climber always has one ready while the ground crew collects the last load.
Stop the brush at the bottom with a soft landing, such as a brush pile, or by having the low end tied off on a friction device so it can be eased.

Check that both sheaves turn freely, side plates are not bent and the axles are tight. Retire after damage or a severe shock load. Speedlines are rigging, not life support, unless the whole system is designed and rated for that use; follow Petzl's instructions and train to ANSI Z133.
Keep the pulley clean of sap and grit, which slows the sheaves and wears the rope faster.

faq.q: What is the difference between a tandem pulley and a double pulley?
faq.a: A tandem has two sheaves in line to ride along a rope. A double has two side by side for building mechanical advantage.

faq.q: Can I use the Tandem on any rope?
faq.a: Use it within the rope diameter range Petzl lists for it.

name: Crosby Chain Choker Hook
title: Crosby Chain Choker Hook for Log Skidding
meta: Crosby chain choker hook for making a sliding choker on logging chain. How choker hooks work for skidding logs and what to check before every pull.
tagline: A choker hook that turns a length of chain into a sliding log choker.
summary: A Crosby chain choker hook slides along a logging chain so you can wrap a log, pull the chain tight and drag it. It is a basic piece of wood-handling hardware for skidding logs to the loader or out of the backyard.
highlights: Turns a length of chain into a sliding choker
Grips the log tighter as you pull
Forged hardware from Crosby
Useful for skidding with a tractor, mini skid steer or winch
specs: Match hook size to chain size

p: Wrap the chain around the log, pass the end back through the choker hook, and hook on to the machine or winch. When you pull, the chain cinches around the log. Release tension and the hook slides loose so you can unwrap.
Set the choker near the end of the log so it lifts slightly and slides instead of plowing into the ground.

A sliding choker is quicker than tying a log hitch every time and holds tighter on round wood. Keep a couple of chokers rigged on chain in the truck for pulling logs out of tight backyards to the loader or onto a trailer.
On a winch line, a short chain with a choker hook saves wear on the winch rope by keeping it off the bark and dirt.
Hooks also save the chain itself from the kinks a knotted chain picks up.

Use a hook matched to your chain size and grade, and keep the working load within the lowest-rated component. Inspect for spread throats, cracks and worn chain contact points. Stand clear of the chain and log when pulling; a chain that slips or breaks can whip. Do not use skidding hardware for overhead lifting unless it is rated for that.
Grease and rust-proof the hardware between jobs.

faq.q: What size choker hook do I need?
faq.a: Match the choker hook to your chain size and grade so it slides correctly and holds the load.

faq.q: Can I use a choker hook for lifting?
faq.a: Only if the hook and chain are rated for overhead lifting. Most choker setups are for skidding.

name: Crosby Chain Connector
title: Crosby Chain Connectors for Chain Repair and Rigging
meta: Crosby chain connectors join chain to chain, hooks or rings without welding. Where an arborist uses a chain connecting link and how to size and inspect one.
tagline: A forged connecting link for joining chain, hooks and rings in the field.
summary: Crosby chain connectors join two pieces of chain, or chain to a hook or ring, without welding. On a tree crew that means building a custom-length skidding chain, repairing a damaged one, or fitting a grab hook to the end.
highlights: Joins chain to chain, hooks or rings
No welding, assemble in the field
Forged hardware from Crosby
Handy for building and repairing skidding chains
specs: Match link to chain size and grade

p: A Crosby chain link is the quick fix when a chain is too short, a hook is damaged, or you want a ring on the end for a winch line. Join the pieces, assemble the link per Crosby's instructions, and the chain is back in service.
Match the connector to the chain size and grade so the weakest point is not the link itself.

They are also useful for linking a winch cable eye to a chain, or adding a shortening hook so one chain covers different log sizes. Keep a few links in the truck bin; a broken chain at the start of a big cleanup is a long trip back to the shop.
Clean and lightly oil connectors before storing them so the pins and bodies do not rust together.

Check connectors for cracks, wear and spread before each use, and replace any that look stretched. The working load of the assembly is that of its lowest-rated part. Use rated alloy components if the chain will ever be used for lifting, and keep chain work clear of people; a failing chain can whip.
Do not grind, heat or weld connecting links; it changes the steel.
Retire any link that will not assemble cleanly.

faq.q: Can I reuse a Crosby chain connector?
faq.a: Follow Crosby's instructions for the specific link. Inspect it before reuse and replace if it is damaged or deformed.

faq.q: Does the connector reduce chain strength?
faq.a: The assembly is limited by its lowest-rated component, so match the link to the chain grade.

name: Galvanized Clevis
title: Galvanized Clevis: Uses, Sizing and Load Ratings
meta: A galvanized clevis connects chain, cable and hardware with a removable pin. How a clevis is used on tree jobs, rated versus unrated hardware, and safe pinning.
tagline: A galvanized pinned connector for chain, cable and hitch work around the yard.
summary: A galvanized clevis is a U-shaped connector closed with a removable pin, used to join chain, cable, rings and hitch points. Around a tree service it shows up on equipment hitches, skidding chains, cable work and anywhere you need a solid, pinned connection.
highlights: U-shaped body with removable pin
Galvanized finish for outdoor use
Connects chain, cable, rings and hitches
Simple, strong and easy to inspect
Choose rated hardware for any critical load
specs: Removable, secured to stop backing out
Connections for chain, cable and hitches
Use only marked, rated hardware for rigging loads

p: A clevis is one of the oldest pieces of connecting hardware. The U-shaped body goes around whatever you are connecting, and a pin closes the open end. Unlike a hook, it cannot come unhooked when the load goes slack, and unlike a carabiner, it is built for steel-on-steel work like chain and hitches.
On a tree crew you will see a clevis on the hitch of a log trailer, at the end of a skidding chain, on cable runs for guying, or holding a snatch block to an anchor strap on a winch setup.

body.h: Clevis, shackle and the difference that matters
p: People use clevis and shackle loosely, and many shapes overlap. What matters for safety is whether the piece is rated. A rated shackle or clevis is marked with its working load and made to a known standard. Generic farm-store clevises are often unmarked, and their strength is unknown.

For hitching and general yard use, a galvanized clevis is fine. For anything that will hold a load over people, anchor a rigging system, or be part of a winch pull near the crew, use hardware with a marked working load limit and stay within it.
Browse rated rings, shackles and connectors in rings and other hardware.

Make sure the pin goes all the way through both ears and is secured with its cotter, clip or nut so it cannot work loose under vibration. A pin that is only half seated, or a threaded pin that has backed out, is a common way connections fail.
Load the clevis in line through the bow and pin. Side-loading the ears bends the body and the pin. Do not substitute a bolt for the proper pin; the grade and fit may be wrong.
Size the clevis so the chain or hardware sits fully in the bow without being forced. A tight fit pries the ears apart under load.
If the pin is hard to start, check for a bent ear or burred threads before forcing it.

Look for bent pins, spread ears, cracks, heavy rust and wear at the bow. Galvanizing slows corrosion but does not stop wear. Replace any clevis that has been overloaded or deformed; steel does not go back into shape safely. Keep the working load of the whole assembly within the rating of its weakest piece, and train the crew on rigging hardware per ANSI Z133.

Store spare clevises and pins together in a bin so pins do not get lost and replaced with bolts in a pinch. A labeled bin of rated hardware next to a separate bin of yard hardware keeps the two from getting mixed up on the truck.
When you buy, note the marking on rated hardware and keep the paperwork. Knowing what a clevis is rated for is what lets you use it with confidence.

faq.q: What is the difference between a clevis and a shackle?
faq.a: The terms overlap. Both are pinned U-shaped connectors. What matters is whether the hardware is marked with a rated working load.

faq.q: Can I use a galvanized clevis for tree rigging?
faq.a: Only if it is marked with a working load limit suitable for the forces involved. Unmarked clevises belong on hitches and general yard work.

faq.q: How do I keep a clevis pin from backing out?
faq.a: Use the correct pin and secure it with its cotter pin, clip or locking nut. Check it during the job.

name: Buckingham Medium Portawrap
title: Buckingham Medium Portawrap Lowering Device
meta: The Buckingham medium Portawrap is a trunk-mounted friction device for lowering wood. How the port a wrap works, how many wraps to take, and how to inspect it.
tagline: A medium friction lowering device for controlled lowering on everyday removals.
summary: The Buckingham medium Portawrap is the classic friction lowering device: a tube with horns that you mount to the trunk and wrap the rigging line around. The ground worker controls how fast each piece comes down by adding wraps and holding tension on the tail. The medium size covers the rope sizes most tree crews rig with day to day.
highlights: Friction lowering device mounted at the base of the tree
Adjust friction by the number of wraps
Horns keep the wraps from riding off
Medium size for common rigging line diameters
Simple design with no moving parts to service
specs: Sling, chain or strap around the trunk
Number of wraps plus tail tension

body.h: How the port a wrap works
p: A port a wrap turns the rigging line's energy into heat through friction on the tube. You anchor the device to the base of the tree or a nearby tree, run the line from the block above down to the tube, and wrap it around between the horns. Each wrap adds friction. The ground worker holds the tail and feeds or stops the line.

Without a lowering device, the friction comes from wraps around the trunk itself, which works but wears the bark and gives you less control. A Portawrap puts the friction in one consistent, inspectable spot and lets you set it to suit the load.
It is the right tool for crews that lower wood regularly but do not need a winch or capstan. See all lowering devices to compare options.

Light pieces need few wraps; heavy pieces and long falls need more. Too few and the ground worker cannot hold the load. Too many and the piece shock-loads the rigging when it stops instead of running a little to soften the catch. The art of rigging is letting pieces run just enough.

Start with more wraps than you think you need while you learn the device, and adjust as you get a feel for each tree. Keep the tail controlled at all times, with gloves on, and never wrap the tail around a hand.
Communication matters as much as wraps. The climber calls the cut, the ground worker confirms ready, and nobody stands between the device and the load. Agree on calls before the first piece.

Mount the Portawrap on the side of the trunk facing the block so the line runs in a straight path from above. Use a sling, chain or strap rated for the forces involved and set it so the device cannot slide up the trunk under load.

Some crews mount it on a neighboring tree to get the ground worker out of the drop zone. That works if the anchor tree is sound and the line runs clear. Keep the area around the device free of brush so the operator has good footing.
Check the tube and horns for grooves worn by rope, cracks and bends. Deep grooves can damage rope and reduce friction control. Inspect the mounting sling or chain every time you set up.

Rigging forces add up fast. Size every component, from block to sling to Portawrap, for the loads you plan to drop. Lowering devices are rigging equipment, not life support. Train ground workers on wraps and line handling before they run the device, and work to ANSI Z133.
Rope wear concentrates on the tube, so rotate which part of the line takes the wraps, and retire rope that shows glazing or heavy fuzzing.

faq.q: What rope size fits the medium Portawrap?
faq.a: The medium is sized for the mid-range rigging lines most crews use. Check Buckingham's listed range for your rope before you buy.

faq.q: Is a Portawrap the same as a port-a-wrap?
faq.a: Yes. Portawrap, port-a-wrap and port a wrap all refer to the same style of friction lowering device.

faq.q: How many wraps should I use?
faq.a: It depends on load weight, fall distance and rope. Start with more friction while learning and reduce as you gain experience.

faq.q: Medium or large Portawrap?
faq.a: Medium suits typical rigging. Choose the large for heavier wood and bigger rope.

name: Good Rigging Control System (GRCS)
title: GRCS Rigging: Good Rigging Control System
h1: GRCS Rigging: Good Rigging Control System
meta: The Good Rigging Control System combines a lowering device and winch for GRCS rigging. How the GRCS works on removals, pulls and lifts, and who needs one.
tagline: A trunk-mounted lowering device and winch in one, for crews that rig big wood.
summary: GRCS rigging means running your lowering line through the Good Rigging Control System, a trunk-mounted unit that combines a friction drum for lowering with a winch for lifting and tensioning. It lets one ground worker lower heavy wood, pull a top over or lift a piece off a roof with the same tool.
highlights: Lowering device and winch in one unit
Mounts to the trunk with straps
Lower, lift, tension and pull with one setup
Removable winch handle
Built for crews rigging heavy wood regularly

p: A standard lowering device only adds friction. The Good Rigging Control System adds a winch drum, so you can also take in rope under load. That opens up jobs that used to need a crane or a lot of people: lifting a cut piece clear of a roof before lowering it, pre-tensioning the rigging line so a top does not drop before it catches, or pulling a leaning tree back over the notch.

When lowering, the rope wraps on the drum like on any friction device and the operator controls descent with the tail. Switch to winching and the same rope can be pulled in with the handle. Nothing gets re-rigged.

The design keeps the operator on the ground with full control. One person can manage what used to take a couple of people heaving on a pull line, and the drum gives them a mechanical advantage that hand-tensioning never could.

Crews doing removals over houses, pools and gardens get the most from a GRCS. Being able to lift a piece rather than letting it swing into a target is a big deal. On take-downs where you need to pull a stem against its lean, a tensioned rigging line through the GRCS can replace a separate pull line and come-along setup.
It is a serious investment and a serious piece of gear. Many crews start with a Portawrap and add a GRCS once their work routinely needs lifting and pre-tensioning.

Strap the unit to the trunk or a nearby anchor tree so the line runs straight from the block to the drum. Follow Good Rigging's manual for wraps, rope size and strapping. Keep the handle off the drum when you are not winching so it cannot spin.
Practice with light loads first. The winch makes it easy to put large forces into the rigging, the block, the sling and the tree itself, and those forces add up faster than most people expect.

Rope choice matters. Use rigging line in the diameter range the manual lists, in good condition, and keep it clean; grit on a winch drum wears rope fast. Watch for heat on long, heavy lowers and give the drum and rope time to cool between big pieces.
Store the unit in a case or secure spot on the truck so the drum and mounting hardware are not knocked around in transport.

Everything in the system must be rated for the loads: rope, block, slings and anchors. Inspect the GRCS, straps and rope before each job. It is rigging equipment, not life support. Operators should be trained on its use, and crews should work to ANSI Z133 with clear communication between climber and ground.

When pre-tensioning a top before the cut, agree on how much tension to apply. Too much can pull the piece off the stub early or split the stem. The climber should be out of the line of any piece that could swing before the operator starts winching.

faq.q: What is GRCS rigging?
faq.a: Rigging run through the Good Rigging Control System, a combined lowering device and winch that mounts to the trunk.

faq.q: Can the GRCS lift loads?
faq.a: Yes. The winch can take in rope under load to lift or tension, within the limits in the manual.

faq.q: Is the GRCS worth it for a small crew?
faq.a: If you routinely rig heavy wood over targets or need to pre-tension and pull, it can replace extra gear and labor. For occasional rigging, a friction device may be enough.

name: Hobbs H2 Lowering Device
title: Hobbs Lowering Device H2 for Heavy Tree Rigging
meta: The Hobbs H2 lowering device mounts to the trunk to control heavy rigging. How a Hobbs lowering device works, who it suits, and how to set it up and inspect it.
tagline: A trunk-mounted friction lowering device built for heavy rigging control.
summary: The Hobbs lowering device H2 is a trunk-mounted friction device built for controlled lowering of heavy wood. It gives the ground worker a big, solid friction surface and positive control of the rigging line, so pieces come down smoothly and stop where they should.
highlights: Mounts to the trunk with straps
Controls heavy rigging loads at the base
Ground worker sets friction by wraps
Rugged build for daily removal work
Keeps friction off the bark of the tree
specs: Strapped to trunk or anchor tree
Wraps on the drum plus tail tension

body.h: How a Hobbs lowering device works
p: Like other friction devices, the Hobbs takes wraps of the rigging line, and the ground worker controls descent by holding the tail. The difference is in the size and build: a larger drum and solid mounting suited to heavier wood than a small tube device handles comfortably.
Mounted at the base, it puts friction in one controlled place instead of on the bark. The operator can let pieces run, then bring them to a smooth stop instead of a hard catch.

Because the device is strapped rather than chained, it sets up fast on trunks of different sizes and comes off cleanly when the removal is done. That matters on days with several removals where every minute spent rigging is a minute not cutting.
It also reduces bark wear on trees you are only pruning, where wrapping the trunk itself would leave scars.

Crews who rig big wood every week get the most from a Hobbs lowering device. If your work is mostly small pruning drops, a large Portawrap may do the job for less money. If you need to lift and pre-tension as well as lower, compare with the Good Rigging Control System, which adds a winch.
Whatever you pick, match the device to the rope diameter and load range in the maker's manual.

Strap the device to the trunk on the side facing the rigging point so the line feeds straight onto the drum. Use straps in good condition and tighten them so the device cannot creep up the stem under load. Some crews prefer to mount on a neighboring tree to keep the operator out of the drop zone; the anchor tree has to be sound.
Clear the ground around the device for good footing. The operator needs room to manage the tail and step back from the line's path.

Keep the rope bag at the operator's feet and the tail running cleanly off the top, so it feeds without snagging when a big piece runs. A snag at the wrong moment turns a smooth lower into a shock load.
Check the drum and horns for rope grooves, cracks and loose hardware, and inspect the straps for cuts and UV damage. Rope wear at the drum is normal, but deep grooves need attention.
All components in a rigging system must be rated for the loads and inspected before use. Lowering devices are not life support. Train operators before they run heavy pieces and work to ANSI Z133.

Agree on calls between climber and ground before the first piece. Keep the device and its straps out of the sun and weather between jobs; UV and moisture shorten strap life. Record inspections so the whole crew knows the gear's history.

faq.q: What is the Hobbs lowering device used for?
faq.a: Controlled lowering of heavy wood during removals, with friction set by the number of wraps on the drum.

faq.q: How is the Hobbs different from a Portawrap?
faq.a: It is a larger, heavier-duty friction device with strap mounting, aimed at crews lowering big wood regularly.

faq.q: Can it lift loads?
faq.a: It is a lowering device. For lifting and pre-tensioning, look at units with a built-in winch such as the GRCS.

name: Large Portawrap Lowering Device
title: Large Porta Wrap Lowering Device for Heavy Rigging
meta: The large porta wrap lowering device handles bigger rope and heavier wood. When to step up from a medium port-a-wrap, how to mount it, and how to set friction.
tagline: The large friction lowering device for bigger rigging lines and heavy wood.
summary: The large porta wrap is the bigger version of the classic friction lowering device, sized for heavier rigging lines and the bigger pieces that go with them. Mount it at the base, take wraps and the ground worker has full control of how fast each piece comes down.
highlights: Large tube for bigger rigging lines
Friction set by number of wraps
Horns keep wraps in place
Simple, no moving parts
Suits crews lowering heavy wood
specs: Sling, chain or strap to trunk

body.h: When to step up to the large size
p: If you are rigging big wood on thicker rope, a medium device starts to run out of room. The large port-a-wrap has the surface and diameter for heavier lines and gives the ground worker more friction to work with. It also suits crews who run long lowers, where the heat built up on a smaller tube becomes an issue.
Smaller crews that mostly do pruning and light removals are usually better served by the medium Portawrap.
A larger tube also spreads heat over more surface, which helps on long lowers. If your rigging line has grown from medium to heavy over the years, the device should grow with it.

Anchor the device to the trunk on the side facing the rigging point, with a sling, chain or strap rated for the load. Set it so it cannot ride up the stem. Wrap the line around the tube between the horns: more wraps for heavier pieces and longer drops, fewer for light ones.

Let pieces run a little before stopping them. A hard stop multiplies the force on the block, the sling and the top of the tree. The ground worker should hold the tail with gloved hands and never wrap it around a hand or arm.

Mount height matters too. Keep the device low enough that the operator can work it standing comfortably, but high enough that the tail does not drag in debris. Set the anchor before the climber goes up so rigging starts without delay.

Friction devices create heat. On long lowers with heavy wood, the rope and tube can get hot enough to glaze rope fibers. Give the system a breather on big jobs, and inspect the rope for glazing and stiffness.
Keep the tube clean of sap and grit, which wears rope faster. A rope bag at the base keeps the tail off the dirt and ready to run.
Wash rope that has been through mud or sawdust, and let it dry before storage. Clean rope grips the tube more predictably, so the ground worker can feel exactly how much friction they have.
Retire rigging rope that shows core damage, flattening or heavy glazing; a lowering device cannot make up for a tired line.

Check the tube and horns for grooves, cracks and bends before each job, along with the mounting hardware. Retire a device with deep grooves that could cut rope. Lowering devices are rigging gear, not life support. Size every component for the load, train the crew, and work to ANSI Z133.
Brief ground workers who are new to the large device. It holds more and stops harder, so they should practice on modest pieces first and learn how quickly heavy wood builds speed on a long drop.

faq.q: What is a porta wrap used for?
faq.a: It adds controlled friction to a rigging line so the ground worker can lower cut pieces smoothly from the tree.

faq.q: Large or medium porta wrap?
faq.a: Choose the large for thicker rope and heavier wood; the medium covers most everyday rigging.

faq.q: Can I put the porta wrap on another tree?
faq.a: Yes, if that tree is sound and the line runs clear. It can keep the operator out of the drop zone.

name: Maasdam Continuous Rope Puller Replacement Handle
title: Maasdam Rope Puller Handle Replacement
meta: Replacement rope puller handle for the Maasdam continuous rope puller. Get a bent or lost handle replaced and the puller back to work pulling trees and logs.
tagline: A replacement handle to get a Maasdam continuous rope puller back to work.
summary: This replacement rope puller handle fits the Maasdam continuous rope puller and gets the tool working again when the original handle is bent, cracked or left behind on a job. The handle is the lever that drives the puller, so a damaged one is worth replacing rather than nursing along.
highlights: Replacement handle for the Maasdam rope puller
Restores full leverage on the puller
Faster than replacing the whole tool
Worth keeping a spare in the truck

p: On a rope puller, the handle is what turns your effort into pulling force. A bent handle can bind, slip off, or fail to give full stroke, and that makes a pull slower and harder to control. A cracked handle can let go under load, which is the last thing you want with a tensioned rope in front of you.
Handles also go missing. They come off for storage, and one left in the grass at a job site is a common story. A spare in the truck bin keeps the puller working.
If you are buying the whole tool, see the Maasdam rope puller kit.

A worn pivot hole is another sign. If the handle wobbles where it attaches, the puller loses stroke and the jaws may not grip consistently. Replacing a twenty-dollar part is much cheaper than fighting a tool all day on a felling job.

Check that the handle matches your Maasdam model before you order. Fit it per Maasdam's instructions, cycle the puller a few strokes without load to confirm smooth action, then make a light test pull before you put it to work on a tree.
Never extend the handle with a pipe or cheater bar. The handle length is matched to the tool's rating; extra leverage overloads the puller and the rope.

If the puller came secondhand, compare the handle to Maasdam's parts listing to confirm you are replacing like with like. Some older tools differ in detail, and a correct fit matters for safe operation. Keep the old handle out of service so nobody grabs it by mistake.
While the handle is off, it is a good moment to look over the jaws and frame.

Keep the puller clean and lightly lubricated as the manual describes. Inspect the jaws or grips that hold the rope, since worn grips can slip. Check the hook, frame and rope for damage before every use.
Store it dry, with the handle stowed so it does not get bent under other gear in the truck. A little care keeps the tool working for years.
Keep a record of when parts were replaced. It helps track how hard the tool is being worked and when it may be time for a full overhaul.

Rope pullers are for pulling and tensioning, not for lifting people. When pulling trees over, keep everyone outside the fall zone and clear of the rope's path if something gives. Size the rope, slings and anchors for the load, and train the crew per ANSI Z133.
Stand to the side of the rope when working the handle, not in line with it, so a slipped grip or broken rope does not come straight back at you.

faq.q: Will this handle fit other rope pullers?
faq.a: It is made for the Maasdam continuous rope puller. Fit on other brands is not assured.

faq.q: Can I use a longer handle for more pull?
faq.a: No. A longer lever overloads the puller and rope. Use the handle supplied for the tool.

faq.q: How do I know my handle needs replacing?
faq.a: Replace it if it is bent, cracked, worn at the pivot, or slips off during use.

name: Maasdam Continuous Rope Puller Kit
title: Maasdam Rope Puller Kit: Rope Come Along for Tree Work
meta: Maasdam rope puller kit, a rope come along for pulling trees, tensioning lines and moving logs. How a continuous rope puller works and how to use it safely.
tagline: A rope come along that pulls any length of rope for tree and yard work.
summary: The Maasdam rope puller is a rope come along: a hand-operated puller that grips rope instead of winding cable on a drum. Because it works on a continuous length of rope, you can pull as far as your rope reaches, which makes it a favorite for pulling trees over, tensioning lines and dragging logs.
highlights: Rope come along with unlimited pull length
Grips the rope with jaws, no drum to fill
Light enough to carry on most jobs
Uses rope instead of steel cable
Good for pulling trees, tensioning and skidding

body.h: How a continuous rope puller works
p: A cable come along winds steel cable onto a drum, and when the drum is full you have to reset. A rope puller instead grips the rope with jaws and pulls it through as you work the handle. The rope passes out the back, so you can keep pulling as long as there is rope left.
Rope is lighter than cable, easier to handle, and kinder to bark when wrapped around a trunk. That is why a rope come along fits so naturally into a tree crew's kit.

The kit format helps too. Rather than buying puller, rope and hooks separately and hoping they match, the kit gives you a working setup on day one. Keep it in a bag in the truck so it is ready when a tree needs a pull.

The common job is helping a tree fall the right way: rope high in the tree, rope puller anchored to another tree or stump out past the fall zone, and steady tension as the sawyer works the back cut. It is also handy for tensioning a speedline, pulling a hung-up top free from a safe distance, or skidding a log into position for bucking.
Pair it with pulleys from our mechanical advantage section to redirect the pull or gain more force.
A rope puller also works as a backup on a stuck saw. If a bar gets pinched in a leaning stem, a little tension from the side can open the kerf enough to free it.

Use rope of the diameter and type the puller is designed for, in good condition. Glazed, cut or crushed rope can slip in the jaws. Anchor the puller to something solid with a rated sling, and keep the line of pull straight.

The force you put on the rope goes into the tree, the anchor and the hardware. Pulling hard on a tree with a weak union or a small anchor tree can cause failures you did not plan for. Think the whole system through before you start cranking.

Use a block or pulley to redirect the pull when the anchor tree is not in line with the direction of fall. A redirect at the base of the anchor tree keeps the puller operator out of the fall zone and lets them work from a comfortable stance.

Rope pullers are not for lifting people or for overhead lifting unless the manual says so. Keep the crew out of the fall zone and the rope's path. Do not extend the handle. Inspect the puller, hook and rope before each job, and train everyone who runs it per ANSI Z133.

Take steady, even strokes rather than hard jerks, and watch the tree as well as the puller. If something looks wrong, such as a crack opening in the wrong place, stop and reassess. Keep a spare handle; a lost or bent one ends the pull.

faq.q: What is a rope come along?
faq.a: A hand-operated puller that grips and pulls rope, rather than winding steel cable on a drum like a cable come along.

faq.q: What rope works with the Maasdam rope puller?
faq.a: Use the rope diameter and type Maasdam specifies. The kit may include rope sized for the puller.

faq.q: Can I use it to pull a tree over?
faq.a: Yes, it is a common use. Anchor out past the fall zone, keep tension steady and keep everyone clear.

name: Petzl Micro Traxion Pulley
title: Petzl Micro Traxion Progress Capture Pulley
meta: The Petzl Micro Traxion is a compact progress capture pulley with a ball-bearing sheave. How arborists use the micro traxion in haul systems and SRT setups.
tagline: A small, efficient progress capture pulley for haul systems and SRT tending.
summary: The Petzl Micro Traxion is a compact pulley with a built-in cam that lets rope run one way and locks it the other. That progress capture makes it the go-to piece for mechanical advantage haul systems, and arborists also use it to tend slack in single-rope climbing setups.
highlights: Built-in cam for progress capture
Sealed ball-bearing sheave runs efficiently
Cam can be locked open to use as a simple pulley
Very compact and light
Popular in haul systems and SRT setups
specs: Marked on the device; see Petzl's instructions

p: In a haul system, every time you reset the pulleys the load wants to slide back. Progress capture holds what you gained. The micro traxion does it in one small device: rope runs freely through the sheave as you pull, and the toothed cam grabs it the instant you let go.
That turns a simple 3:1 setup into something one person can run efficiently, pulling a tree over, tensioning a line or lifting a piece back onto a trailer.

Its efficiency is part of the appeal. A ball-bearing sheave wastes less of your effort than a carabiner or bushing pulley, so more of what you put in reaches the load. Over a long haul, that difference is noticeable in your arms.

body.h: How arborists use the Micro Traxion
p: Beyond haul systems, climbers use it in SRT. Paired with a rope wrench or mechanical device, it can tend slack so the climber does not have to hand-feed rope through the friction device on the way up. Some climbers also use it as part of a foot or knee ascender setup.

Any use in a life-support system must follow Petzl's instructions and the configuration the maker describes, and climbers should be trained before using it that way. Check that your rope's diameter falls within the range Petzl lists.
Because it is small and light, many climbers just leave one on the saddle. When a pull line needs tensioning or a stuck rope needs a haul, it is already there.
It packs small enough to live on the saddle.

The cam's teeth grip the rope sheath. Shock loading or a fall onto a toothed cam can damage the sheath, so keep it in systems where it is used as designed. Keep teeth clean of sap and grit with a brush; clogged teeth grip poorly.
