Lock the cam open with its catch when you want a plain pulley. It is one of the reasons this piece is so versatile: one device, two jobs.
More pulleys and haul gear are in the mechanical advantage section.

Wash it in fresh water after muddy or sappy jobs and let it dry before storage. Do not oil the cam teeth, since lubricant attracts grit and reduces grip. A light drop on the cam pivot, per Petzl's guidance, keeps the action smooth.

Before each use, check the sheave turns freely, the cam springs back and grips, the teeth are not worn or clogged, and the side plates and attachment hole show no cracks or wear. Retire the device if anything looks wrong or after a severe fall load. Follow ANSI Z133 and Petzl's instructions for life-support use.
Write the purchase date on your gear log; Petzl's instructions cover lifespan and inspection frequency, and a record makes those checks easy to keep up with.

faq.q: What is the Petzl Micro Traxion used for?
faq.a: Progress capture in haul systems, and as a slack-tending pulley in SRT climbing setups.

faq.q: What rope diameter fits the Micro Traxion?
faq.a: Petzl lists it for ropes about 8 to 11 mm. Check the current instructions for your rope.

faq.q: Can I use it as a regular pulley?
faq.a: Yes. Lock the cam open and it runs as a simple pulley.

faq.q: Can the Micro Traxion catch a fall?
faq.a: It is not designed as fall arrest. Use it only in the configurations Petzl describes.

name: Port-a-Wrap with Soft Anchor Rigging Sling
title: Port-a-Wrap with Soft Anchor Rigging Sling Kit
h1: Port-a-Wrap with Soft Anchor Rigging Sling
meta: A port-a-wrap friction lowering device paired with a soft anchor rigging sling for mounting it to the trunk. A ready rigging kit for crews lowering wood.
tagline: A friction lowering device and soft anchor sling, ready to mount and rig.
summary: This kit pairs a port-a-wrap friction lowering device with a soft anchor rigging sling, so you have the device and the means to mount it in one purchase. Wrap the sling around the trunk, clip the port-a-wrap on, and the ground worker is ready to lower.
highlights: Friction lowering device plus mounting sling
Soft sling is kind to bark
Quick to set up at the base of the tree
Good starter rigging kit for growing crews
specs: Port-a-wrap and soft anchor rigging sling

body.h: Why buy it as a kit
p: A lowering device is only as good as its anchor. A soft sling spreads load over the bark, is easy to adjust for different trunk sizes, and packs small. Buying the two together means the sling is sized for the job rather than something grabbed from the truck.
It is a sensible first rigging setup for a crew moving from roping down limbs on a natural crotch to controlled lowering.
The soft sling also comes off easily when the job is done and packs into the same bag as the device, so the whole setup lives together on the truck. Nothing gets left behind at the base of a tree.
Wrap the sling around the trunk on the side facing the rigging point and connect the port-a-wrap so the line runs straight onto the tube. Take wraps to suit the load and keep the tail under control.

Inspect the sling for cuts, abrasion and UV fading, and the device for grooves and cracks, before every job. Lowering gear is rigging, not life support. Train ground workers on wraps and line handling, and follow ANSI Z133.
Size the setup to the work: this kit suits everyday rigging, while very heavy wood calls for larger devices and slings.

faq.q: What is a port-a-wrap?
faq.a: A friction lowering device mounted at the base of the tree. Rope wraps around it so the ground worker can control descent.

faq.q: Why use a soft sling to mount it?
faq.a: It adapts to trunk size, protects bark and is easy to carry and inspect.

name: Weaver Speed Line Kit
title: Weaver Speed Line Kit for Arborist Brush Removal
meta: The Weaver speed line kit puts the rope and hardware for a speedline in one bag. How a speed line moves brush to the drop zone, how to rig it, and safe limits.
tagline: A packaged speedline setup from Weaver for zipping brush to the drop zone.
summary: A speed line lets you send brush down a tensioned rope from the canopy to a landing spot well away from the tree, and the Weaver speedline kit packages what you need to rig one. It is the answer for removals where the drop zone under the tree is crowded with roofs, decks and plantings.
highlights: Packaged speedline setup from Weaver
Moves brush over targets to a clear landing zone
Speeds cleanup by landing brush in one spot
Keeps lowering line free for wood
Comes together in one bag for the truck
specs: High in tree, low at landing zone

p: On a tight lot, getting brush to the ground is easy. Getting it to the ground without hitting the house, the fence and the flower beds is the hard part. A speed line runs from a high anchor in the tree to a low anchor at the landing zone, and each bundle of brush slides down it, clearing everything underneath.

It changes the pace of a job. The climber keeps cutting and sending, the ground crew keeps clearing the landing zone, and the brush ends up next to the chipper instead of spread across the yard. Meanwhile the main lowering line stays free for wood.

It is also a cleaner job for the client. Fewer crushed shrubs and dented gutters means fewer callbacks and a better reputation for the crew. Many arborists who try a speed line on one tight job end up keeping a kit in the truck permanently.

Pick the high anchor above the work in sound wood, and the low anchor at the landing zone: a stump, another tree or a ground anchor your company approves. The line angle sets the speed. A steep line delivers fast and hard; a shallow one may stall loads halfway.

Tension the line with a mechanical advantage system or with wraps on a lowering device at the low end. A controllable low anchor lets you slacken the line to bring loads down gently into the pile. Over-tensioning multiplies forces on both anchors, so tension only enough to clear the targets.
For a store-assembled alternative, compare the speed line kit with carabiners.
Protect the bark at the high anchor with a sling or friction saver rather than running the line around a bare limb, and use a sling sized for the forces a loaded speed line can put on it.

Clip a pulley or carabiner to the line first, then to the brush with a sling. Keep loads small and trimmed so they ride clean. Several light bundles are easier on the anchors and the crew than one heavy limb. Have extra connectors on the line so the climber is not waiting for gear to come back.

Everyone stays out from under the line and the landing zone while loads are moving. Agree on calls for sending, clear and stop. If a load hangs up halfway, do not stand under it to free it; use the low anchor to slack and lower it.
Strip awkward side branches so bundles ride without catching. A tangle of twigs dragging along the line slows everything and wears the rope.

A speed line is rigging, not a life-support system. Never clip a person to it. Check the rope, slings, pulleys and carabiners before every job, and retire anything cut, glazed or deformed. Re-check the anchors and tension after the first few loads, since rope stretches and slings settle.
Train the crew to set up and run a speed line before using one over property, and work to ANSI Z133. The line cuts a job's risk only when everyone knows how it works and where to stand.

faq.q: What is a speed line in tree work?
faq.a: A tensioned rope from a high anchor in the tree to a low anchor at the landing zone, used to slide brush away from targets.

faq.q: How steep should a speed line be?
faq.a: Steep enough that loads slide without stalling, shallow enough that they arrive under control. A controllable low anchor lets you adjust.

faq.q: Can I send wood down a speed line?
faq.a: Light wood, yes. Heavy pieces put large forces on the anchors; use the lowering line for those.

name: 3/4" Whoopie Sling
title: 3/4" Whoopie Sling for Heavy Rigging Anchors
meta: The 3/4 in whoopie sling is an adjustable rope sling for heavy rigging anchors. How a whoopie sling adjusts, why sailors and arborists use them, and inspection.
tagline: An adjustable 3/4 in rope sling for anchoring heavy rigging blocks.
summary: A 3/4 in whoopie sling is an adjustable rope sling made from hollow-braid rope, with a fixed eye at one end and an adjustable eye at the other. Arborists use them to hang heavy rigging blocks on trunks of any size, and the same design is popular in sailing for adjustable rigging.
highlights: Adjustable length fits a wide range of trunk sizes
3/4 in diameter for heavy rigging
Hollow-braid construction adjusts by hand
Fixed eye and adjustable eye

p: A whoopie sling uses a hollow-braid rope buried inside itself. Slide the bury to make the adjustable eye larger or smaller; under load the outer braid squeezes down on the inner section and holds. The result is one sling that fits a small stem or a big trunk without wasting length or wraps.
Sailors use the same trick for adjustable shrouds and lashings, which is why you see the term whoopie sling with sailing. In tree work the 3/4 in size is for heavy rigging blocks and big wood.

Because it adjusts, one whoopie can do the work of several fixed-length slings, which saves space and weight in the rigging bag. It is also kind to bark, since there is no long tail wrapped around the trunk.

Wrap the trunk, pass the fixed eye through the adjustable eye or connect with a shackle or carabiner, and snug it down. Make sure the adjustable section has the minimum bury the maker specifies before loading.

Check for cuts, abrasion, glazing and stiff or crushed spots before each use. Retire a sling that has been overloaded. Rigging slings are not life support; size every part of the system for the load and work to ANSI Z133.

faq.q: Why is it called a whoopie sling?
faq.a: It is a traditional name for an adjustable buried-braid sling, used for years in sailing and now common in tree rigging.

faq.q: 3/4 in or 5/8 in whoopie sling?
faq.a: The 3/4 in suits heavy rigging and big blocks. The 5/8 in is lighter for everyday rigging.

name: 5/8" Whoopie Sling
title: 5/8" Whoopie Sling: Adjustable Arborist Rigging Sling
meta: The 5/8 in whoopie sling is an adjustable arborist rigging sling for blocks and lowering devices. How it adjusts, how to set it on a trunk, and when to retire.
tagline: An adjustable 5/8 in rope sling for hanging blocks on any trunk size.
summary: The 5/8 in whoopie sling is an adjustable arborist rigging sling: a hollow-braid rope with a fixed eye and an adjustable eye, sized for the everyday rigging most crews do. One sling fits stems from small to large, so you carry fewer slings and set blocks faster.
highlights: Adjusts by hand to fit different trunk sizes
5/8 in diameter for everyday rigging
Fixed eye and adjustable eye
Lighter than heavy-duty 3/4 in slings
Packs small in the rigging bag
specs: Hanging rigging blocks and lowering devices

p: A fixed-length sling either fits the trunk or it does not. Too long and you are taking wraps to use up the extra; too short and it will not go round. A whoopie sling adjusts. Pull the adjustable eye open, wrap the stem, choke or connect it, then slide it tight. Under load the braid grips itself and holds.
That flexibility is why the whoopie sling is one of the most common arborist slings. It handles block anchors high in the tree, base anchors for lowering devices, and redirects, all with one piece.

Compared with steel chain or webbing, rope slings are lighter, easier on bark and simpler to inspect by hand. A couple of 5/8 in whoopies in the bag handle most of what a typical residential crew rigs in a day.

Wrap the sling around the stem above a branch collar or crotch that will stop it sliding down, then pass the eye through or connect the eyes with a carabiner or shackle rated for the load. Slide the adjustable eye down until it is snug. Choked around the trunk, it bites tighter as load comes on.
Hang the block so the rigging line runs cleanly without rubbing the sling. When removing, slack the sling fully before trying to slide the eye open.
See other adjustable slings in the adjustable slings section, including the heavier 3/4 in version.

On a tree you are pruning rather than removing, set the sling over a protective layer or choose a spot where the bark is thick, and avoid sawing the sling around under load, which scuffs bark and wears the sling. On removals, set it where the stem is sound and large enough for the forces the block will see.
Some climbers like to pre-set the whoopie on the ground at roughly the right size, then fine-tune it once it is around the stem, saving time aloft.
A whoopie needs its minimum bury to hold. Never adjust the sling so short that the buried section is less than the maker's minimum. Some slings mark the limit; respect it.
Dirt and sap inside the braid make adjustment stiff and can wear fibers from the inside. Wash slings in clean water when they get filthy and let them dry out of the sun.
Store slings coiled loosely in a bag away from fuel, bar oil and battery acid. Chemicals can weaken synthetic fibers without much visible sign, and the truck bed is where that kind of damage happens.

Before each job, run the sling through your hands and look for cuts, pulled strands, glazing from friction, stiff or flattened spots and discoloration from chemicals. Check the eyes and the adjustable section closely, since that is where wear concentrates.
Retire a sling that has been shock loaded beyond its rating or shows damage. Rigging slings are not life support. Size every component for the load, and train crews to ANSI Z133.
Keep a simple log of each sling's purchase date and any heavy loads it has caught. When in doubt, retire it; a new sling costs far less than a failure.

faq.q: What is a whoopie sling used for in tree work?
faq.a: Anchoring rigging blocks, lowering devices and redirects to trunks of different sizes with one adjustable sling.

faq.q: How does a whoopie sling hold its adjustment?
faq.a: The outer braid squeezes the buried inner section under load, gripping it so the eye does not slip.

faq.q: How short can I adjust a whoopie sling?
faq.a: Only down to the minimum bury the maker specifies. Shorter than that, it may not hold.

name: 5/8" x 20' Premium Crane Sling
title: 5/8" x 20' Premium Crane Sling for Tree Picks
meta: The 5/8 in x 20 ft premium crane sling is a rope sling for crane-assisted removals. How crews choke and set a crane sling on picks, and what to inspect daily.
tagline: A 5/8 in x 20 ft rope sling for setting chokers on crane-assisted removals.
summary: This 5/8 in x 20 ft premium crane sling is a rope sling for choking pieces on crane-assisted tree removal. The 20 ft length wraps big wood with room to spare, and rope is easier on the climber's hands and the tree than steel.
highlights: 5/8 in rope sling for crane picks
20 ft length wraps large stems
Eyes at each end for choking and hooking
Lighter to carry aloft than chain or steel

body.h: How crews use a crane sling
p: On a crane removal, the climber sets one or two slings on each pick, choked around the piece above its balance point, and hooks the eye onto the crane hook. The crane takes tension before the cut so the piece is supported the moment it comes free.
A 20 ft sling gives you enough length to choke a large stem or wrap a wide top. Rope is lighter to carry up the tree than steel and does not bite into the climber's gloves.
Many crews carry a matched pair so the climber can set two chokers on long or unbalanced pieces, controlling how the pick hangs once it is free.
Mark your crane slings so they are not mixed in with everyday rigging gear.

Crane work involves high, sudden loads. Know the weight of each pick, and use slings with a rated capacity for the hitch you are using; a choker hitch carries less than a straight vertical pull. Follow the crane operator's and qualified rigger's direction on every pick.
Inspect crane slings daily for cuts, abrasion, heat damage and missing or unreadable tags, and remove damaged slings from service. Follow ANSI Z133 and the crane safety rules that apply to your work.
Store crane slings clean and dry, coiled loosely, away from fuel and bar oil. Keep the tags legible, and replace a sling whose tag is missing even if it looks fine.

faq.q: What is a crane sling used for in tree work?
faq.a: It chokes cut pieces so a crane can hold and lift them free during a removal.

faq.q: Does a choker hitch reduce sling capacity?
faq.a: Yes. A choker hitch has a lower rated capacity than a vertical hitch. Check the sling's tag.

name: Endless Loop Round Slings
title: Endless Loop Round Slings for Tree Rigging and Cranes
meta: Endless round slings are soft polyester slings for crane picks and heavy rigging. How a round sling is rated by color, how to pick a hitch, and how to inspect.
tagline: Soft endless polyester slings for crane picks, rigging anchors and lifts.
summary: Round slings are endless loops of load-bearing polyester fiber inside a protective cover. They are soft, flexible and grip wood well, which makes them a favorite for crane-assisted removals, heavy rigging anchors and lifting logs with a loader or excavator.
highlights: Endless loop, use any part of the sling
Soft cover protects bark and grips wood
Color-coded by rated capacity
Light and flexible for carrying aloft
Works in vertical, choker and basket hitches

body.h: Why tree crews use round slings
p: An endless sling has no eyes to wear out and no fixed contact point. You can rotate it so a different section takes the load each time, which spreads wear. The soft cover conforms to the wood and grips, and it is gentle on bark when you anchor a block to a tree you are keeping.
On crane removals, round slings are fast to set: choke the piece, drop the loop over the hook and go. With a loader or excavator, they wrap logs without the steel-on-wood slipping you get with chain.
They also pack small. A few round slings take up less room in the truck than the equivalent steel, and they do not rust or kink.

body.h: Reading capacity and choosing a hitch
p: Round slings are usually color-coded by rated capacity, and each sling carries a tag with its ratings for vertical, choker and basket hitches. The color helps you pick the right sling quickly, but the tag is what counts. A sling with a missing or unreadable tag should come out of service.

Hitch choice changes capacity. A choker hitch is rated well below vertical; a basket hitch can be rated higher if the legs are near vertical. Wide sling angles reduce capacity fast. Pick a sling with margin for the hitch you will use, and remember that tree work brings dynamic loads that static lifting tables do not show.
For rope-based crane slings, see the 5/8 in x 20 ft crane sling.

When a pick needs two slings, set them so the piece hangs as planned once cut. A choker set too close to the end lets the piece tip; one set near the balance point keeps it level. Talk through each pick with the crane operator and the ground crew before the cut.

The cover protects the core, but a chainsaw cuts through both instantly. Keep the saw well clear of slings, and never cut a piece with the sling across your cut line. Sharp edges, such as metal or a freshly cut stub, can cut a loaded round sling; use wear pads where needed.
Keep round slings away from heat and chemicals. Bar oil, fuel and battery acid can weaken polyester. Store them dry, out of the sun, in a bag or bin.

Before each use, check the cover for cuts, holes and burns, and feel for knots, lumps or soft spots in the core. Exposed core yarns mean the sling is done. Look for melted or discolored areas from friction.
Retire any sling that is damaged or has been overloaded. Follow the maker's instructions, applicable sling standards and ANSI Z133 for tree work.

Keep a log of the slings on the truck and when each was put into service. Round slings tend to get used hard on crane days, and a record helps you spot the ones due for closer inspection. Clean mud off with fresh water and let them dry before packing.

faq.q: What is the difference between a round sling and an endless sling?
faq.a: Round slings are a type of endless sling: a loop of polyester yarns inside a cover. Endless slings can also be webbing.

faq.q: What do round sling colors mean?
faq.a: Colors are commonly used to indicate rated capacity, but always confirm with the tag on the sling.

faq.q: Can I use a round sling to anchor a rigging block?
faq.a: Yes, if its rating suits the forces involved. Use wear protection on sharp edges.

name: 1/2" Bull Rope Rigging Sling
title: 1/2" Bull Rope Rigging Sling for Block Anchors
meta: A 1/2 in bull rope rigging sling, the bull tail for tying off blocks and hanging pieces. How to choose a bull tail for rigging and inspect it before each job.
tagline: A 1/2 in rope sling, or bull tail, for anchoring blocks and tying off pieces.
summary: This 1/2 in bull rope rigging sling is a length of rigging rope with an eye spliced in one end, often called a bull tail. Arborists use it to anchor rigging blocks with a timber hitch or wraps, to tie off pieces, and as an all-purpose rigging connection.
highlights: Spliced eye at one end, tail at the other
Ties to the tree with wraps and hitches
1/2 in rope for light to moderate rigging
Versatile, adjusts to any trunk size
Easy to inspect by hand

p: Bull tail rigging is one of the oldest setups in tree work. A short length of strong rope with a spliced eye is tied around the stem, usually with a series of wraps and a timber hitch, cow hitch or similar knot, and the block is clipped to the eye. Because the tail is tied rather than fixed length, it fits any trunk size.
Bull rope, the strong double-braid line used for rigging, is what these slings are made from. In 1/2 in it suits light to moderate rigging: pruning drops, small removals and redirects.

It is also the sling to use when you are short on gear. A spare bull tail can stand in for a fixed sling, a tag line anchor or a pull-line tie-off, which is why many climbers keep one clipped to the saddle.

Wrap the stem enough times to spread the load and stop the sling sliding, then finish with a hitch you were trained on. Leave a reasonable tail. The eye should hang where the block can run without the rigging line rubbing the trunk.
A bull tail is also handy for tying off a piece before the cut, setting a natural crotch redirect, or anchoring a lowering device on a small tree. See other options in heavy-duty slings.

Dress the wraps neatly so they lie flat and share the load. Crossed or bunched wraps can slip or pinch. When the job is done, the tied wraps come off quickly, which is part of why bull tails are still popular after decades of new gear.
For heavier wood, step up to a larger diameter or to a dedicated whoopie or loopie sling. A 1/2 in bull tail is the light end of the range, chosen because it is quick to tie and easy to carry.
Match the sling's rating to the forces in your rigging, not just the weight of the piece. A dropped piece stopped suddenly can put several times its weight into the block and sling.

Some crews keep a few lengths: a short bull tail for limbs and a longer one for big stems. Mark each one so it is easy to grab the right length from the bag. Spliced eyes should be made by someone trained to splice that rope type.

Check the splice for pulled or loose tucks, and the rope for cuts, glazing, flattened sections and chemical stains. Retire a sling that has been overloaded or shows core damage. Rigging slings are not life support. Work to ANSI Z133.
Store it clean and dry with the rest of the rigging gear, and keep it out of the sun when not in use.
Never use a rigging bull tail as part of a climbing system.

faq.q: What is a bull tail in tree rigging?
faq.a: A spliced-eye rope sling that is tied around the stem to anchor a block or tie off a piece.

faq.q: Is 1/2 in rope enough for a rigging sling?
faq.a: For light to moderate rigging, yes, within its rating. Use larger slings for heavier wood.

faq.q: What knot do I use to tie off a bull tail?
faq.a: Several wraps finished with a timber hitch or similar hitch is common. Use a hitch you have been trained on and dress it well.

name: Heavy Duty Webbing Slings
title: Heavy Duty Webbing Sling for Tree Rigging
meta: A heavy duty webbing sling is a flat sewn arborist sling for block anchors, log lifts and rigging redirects. How to choose one and inspect it before each job.
tagline: Flat sewn webbing slings for block anchors, log lifts and redirects.
summary: A heavy duty webbing sling is a flat strap of sewn synthetic webbing that wraps the trunk or a log and grips well. Arborists use webbing slings to anchor blocks, set redirects, and lift or drag logs, and they lie flat against bark for less wear on trees you are keeping.
highlights: Flat webbing spreads load across bark
Sewn eyes for connecting hardware
Light and easy to carry
Works as anchor, choker or basket sling

p: Flat webbing is a good arborist sling where you want grip and bark protection. It wraps a stem or a log like a belt, so it spreads pressure and is less likely to slide. Use one as a block anchor on trees you are pruning, as a choker on logs for the loader, or as a basket around a short round.
Webbing packs flat and dries quickly, and a few in the truck cover a lot of jobs.
Webbing also works well for lifting logs with a loader or excavator, where its wide contact grips bark and reduces slipping. Pick lengths that suit the diameters you usually handle.
Keep them separate from climbing gear.

Each sling carries a tag with its rated capacity by hitch. Choose a sling with margin for the hitch and the dynamic loads of tree work. Keep chainsaws and sharp edges well away; webbing cuts easily under load.
Before each use, check for cuts, burns, broken stitching, holes and a readable tag. Retire damaged slings. Rigging slings are not life support; follow ANSI Z133.
Store webbing out of sunlight, since UV weakens synthetic fibers over time.
Wash muddy slings in clean water and let them dry before packing.

faq.q: Webbing sling or rope sling?
faq.a: Webbing grips and spreads load across bark; rope slings handle abrasion and are easier to adjust and inspect.

faq.q: What does the tag on a webbing sling mean?
faq.a: It lists rated capacities for each hitch type. A sling without a readable tag should be removed from service.

name: CMI Heavy Duty Loop Runners
title: CMI Heavy Duty Loop Runner Slings
meta: CMI heavy duty loop runners are sewn webbing loops for anchors, redirects and light rigging. How arborists use a loop runner and what to check before each job.
tagline: Sewn webbing loops for quick anchors, redirects and light rigging.
summary: A CMI heavy duty loop runner is a sewn loop of webbing that you girth hitch, basket or choke around a limb to make a quick anchor. Arborists use loop runners for redirects, light rigging, anchoring pulleys and gear on the ground.
highlights: Sewn webbing loop, no knots to tie
Girth hitch, basket or choke around limbs
Light and quick to carry on the saddle
CMI build quality

body.h: How arborists use a loop runner
p: A loop runner is the quickest anchor you can carry. Girth hitch it around a limb and clip a pulley for a redirect, or basket it around a stub to anchor a light rigging point. On the ground, use it to anchor a pulley at the base of a tree for a pull line.
Because they are sewn, there is no knot to untie after a load, and they weigh almost nothing on the saddle.
Carry a few in different lengths so you can wrap both small limbs and larger stems. Color-coding by length makes it easy to grab the right one from the saddle.
They also make tidy gear loops on the ground.

Girth hitches reduce a runner's strength compared with a straight pull, and sharp edges reduce it more. Check the marking for its rating and use runners within it. Inspect the stitching and webbing for cuts, burns and fraying before use.
If a runner is part of a climbing system, it must be rated for life support and used as CMI instructs. Keep rigging and climbing gear separate, and train to ANSI Z133.
Wash dirty runners in clean water and air dry them.
Retire any runner with a faded or missing marking.

faq.q: What is a loop runner?
faq.a: A sewn loop of webbing used as a quick sling for anchors and redirects.

faq.q: Can I use a loop runner for climbing?
faq.a: Only if it is rated for life support and used per CMI's instructions. Keep rigging runners separate.
